Websites must remain accessible when tracking cookies are refused 07 March 2019 Themes: Cookies Big data and profiling Websites that only grant visitors access to their site if they agree to the placement of so-called 'tracking cookies' or other similar methods of tracking and recording behavior by means of software or other digital methods, do not comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) published this clarification of standards today. The AP received dozens of complaints from website visitors who, after refusing tracking cookies, were denied access to the web pages they wanted to consult. The AP will therefore intensify its monitoring of proper compliance and has already sent a letter to a number of specific parties regarding this matter. Tracking software "Digitally tracking and recording browsing behavior on the internet via tracking software or other digital methods is one of the largest processing activities of personal data, as almost everyone is active on the internet. To protect privacy, it is therefore important that parties request consent from website visitors in a proper manner," says Aleid Wolfsen, chairman of the AP. "This way, people can consciously and properly exercise their right to the protection of personal data.

If a website requests consent for tracking cookies and, upon refusal, access to the website or service is not possible, people are pressured into providing their personal data, and that is unlawful." Only with consent Under the rules of the GDPR, organizations must have a legal basis to process personal data. If companies wish to track individuals with tracking cookies, tracking software, or other digital methods, they must request consent for this. This is for good reason; website visitors must be able to trust that their personal data is properly protected, according to the rules of privacy law. Many websites therefore request prior consent for the placement of various 'tracking software' such as tracking cookies, tracking pixels, or fingerprinting. There is no objection to software for the proper functioning of the website and general analysis of visits to that site. More in-depth tracking and analysis of website visitor behavior and sharing this information with other parties is only permitted with consent. That consent must be able to be given completely freely.

AP Netherlands - Tracking cookies

**Tracking cookies** Tracking cookies make it possible to monitor the internet behavior of website visitors across different websites with the aim of treating them differently, for example by showing personalized advertisements or offers. Tracking cookies make it possible to create profiles of individuals (profiling). Personal data is processed with tracking cookies. **On this page** **Complying with the GDPR with tracking cookies** Do you process personal data of visitors to your website with tracking cookies? Then you must comply with the rules of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The most important requirements are that you: * have a legal basis for the data processing; * inform visitors in a timely and proper manner about the processing of personal data and the purpose of the processing; * adequately secure the (personal) data. To obtain valid consent for placing tracking cookies, you must inform your website visitors about: * the (types of) personal data you collect and process via the cookies; * the purposes of the data processing; * the recipients and how many recipients there are (or the categories of recipients) to whom you provide the data; * the withdrawal of consent; * all other information necessary to give your visitors a fair picture of the data processing. **Tip:** Do you want to check your website? The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has a free website audit program.

The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) has a free website audit program. This program shows, for example, which cookies your website uses, whether visitor data is forwarded, and whether your website uses a secure connection. The program is available in English. **Collection and processing of personal data** Provide information about the types of personal data you collect and process with tracking cookies. This includes, at a minimum: * visited web pages; * IP addresses; * cookie content; * referrer URL; * any other data you collect, such as data about the peripherals used and software settings on the device. **Purposes of data processing** Let your visitors know why you collect and process their personal data. Cookies Cookies are small files that a website or app owner places on your device, such as a computer, smartphone, or tablet. This happens when you visit a website or use an app. On this page General information Some cookies are necessary for a website or app to function properly (functional cookies). With cookies, the owner of the website or app can collect and store information about your visit, or about you as a visitor. For example, what your interests are, how healthy you are, and which political party you vote for. If you do not consent to cookies, you can still use most websites and apps normally. Types of cookies There are 3 types of cookies: functional cookies; limited analytical cookies; other cookies. Functional cookies Functional cookies ensure that a website or app functions correctly. For example, they remember your login details, language preferences, and products in your shopping cart. Consent For placing functional cookies, a website or app owner does not need your consent. However, the owner must inform you that the cookies are being placed. You can find this information, for example, in the privacy statement of the website or app. Limited analytical cookies Limited analytical cookies collect information about visits to a website or app, such as the number of visitors and the most visited pages. This information helps website or app owners improve them. These cookies should not have significant consequences for your privacy.

Consent If limited analytical cookies have no or minimal consequences for your privacy, then a website owner does not need your consent to place these cookies. This is stated in the Telecommunications Act (Article 11.7a). Do limited analytical cookies process your personal data? For this, the website owner needs a legal basis. The use of this type of cookie must also be mentioned in the privacy statement of the website or app. Other cookies Other cookies are cookies that do not fit into the above categories. These cookies often also process personal data. A well-known example of other cookies is tracking cookies. Tracking cookies Tracking cookies monitor your internet behavior. This happens not only on one website but also on other websites and apps you visit and use. Tracking cookies can therefore follow you across multiple websites and apps. By mapping your behavior across multiple websites and apps, tracking cookies can create profiles of you. For example, regarding your interests, political preference, and family situation. AP Netherlands - GDPR Legal Bases Explained

Lawful Bases GDPR explained Each time you process personal data, it constitutes an infringement on the privacy of the individuals concerned. Therefore, you may only process personal data if it is truly unavoidable. That is: if you cannot achieve your purpose without these data. This means you must have a valid reason to process personal data. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) lists 6 such reasons. The legal term for these reasons is 'lawful bases'. You therefore need a lawful basis to be permitted to process personal data. On this page General information on GDPR lawful bases You must assess for yourself which lawful basis applies to you. This is your own responsibility. The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) cannot advise you on this. You determine the lawful basis before you start processing data. The 6 lawful bases The GDPR lists the following 6 lawful bases for processing personal data: You have the consent of the individual concerned. It is necessary to process data to perform a contract. It is necessary to process data because you are legally obliged to do so. It is necessary to process data to protect vital interests. It is necessary to process data to perform a task carried out in the public interest / in the exercise of official authority. It is necessary to process data to pursue your legitimate interest.

Then it is advisable to state the lawful basis in the following places: In your privacy statement. This way, the individuals whose data you process know why you are permitted to do so. And they will not be taken by surprise. This can help you meet your information obligation. In your privacy policy (if you have one, as not every organisation is required to have a privacy policy). You may rely on this lawful basis if you have a contract with someone and you cannot perform that contract without also processing personal data. This lawful basis also applies to the phase before you conclude a contract. For example, if you prepare a quote upon request. For more information about this lawful basis, read the EDPB Guidelines on the lawful basis of contract in the context of online services. Please note: Do not process personal data that is not necessary for the performance of the contract. If you do, you must also have consent or another lawful basis for that processing. Unless you can invoke an exception. The GDPR lists 10 exceptions. In addition, you must have one of the lawful bases for processing 'ordinary' personal data. In practice, some of these exceptions and lawful bases overlap. For example, if you have received explicit consent from the data subject. Of the 10 exceptions in the GDPR, 5 only apply if a legal basis has been created for them in national law. This means you can only invoke such an exception if a Dutch law explicitly permits it. The 10 exceptions are: An individual has given explicit consent for the processing of their own personal data. Only if stipulated by law: The processing is necessary for the purposes of carrying out obligations or exercising specific rights of you or the data subject. This applies in the field of employment law, social security law, or social protection law. The processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person. This only applies when that person is physically or legally incapable of giving consent.

AP Netherlands - Clear cookie banners

Clear Cookie Banners When people visit a website, they often see a cookie banner (also called a cookie notification or cookie pop-up). With a cookie banner, an organization explains to website visitors how their personal data is collected using cookies, and why. On this page With a cookie banner, website visitors can choose which cookies they do or do not want to consent to. It is important that they maintain control over their personal data. In practice, organizations still often request consent in a misleading way. For example, by automatically ticking options. On this page, you will therefore find some guidelines, examples of clear cookie banners, and examples of how not to do it. Cookies and the GDPR There are different types of cookies. As an organization, do you use tracking cookies or similar tracking techniques? Then you can assume that you are processing personal data. You also process personal data with some functional and limited analytical cookies. In that case, you must comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). How do you create a clear cookie banner? The AP highlights 9 important aspects of cookie banners. These 9 guidelines help you create a good cookie banner. Additionally, you must always verify yourself whether you comply with all requirements in the GDPR when processing personal data with cookies.

AP Netherlands - Clear cookie banners

These 9 guidelines help you create a good cookie banner. Additionally, you must always verify yourself whether you comply with all requirements in the GDPR when processing personal data with cookies. The guidelines are: Provide information about the processing of personal data and the purpose of the processing Do not automatically check boxes Use clear text Place different choices on one layer Do not hide certain choices Do not make someone click extra Do not use an inconspicuous link in the text Make withdrawing consent as easy as giving consent Do not confuse consent with legitimate interest Below you will find explanations and examples. Please note: The examples and texts in the images are fictional and intended for illustration. The examples consistently show a part of a clear cookie banner. What exactly needs to be in your banner depends on how you use cookies and process personal data. Provide information about the (type of) personal data and for which purposes it is processed Provide your website visitor with the information necessary to make an informed choice. This includes explaining for which purposes you use cookies and what (type of) personal data you process, before someone makes a choice. Does your website process a lot of personal data for many different purposes? Then it may be appropriate to work with a 2-layer cookie banner. In the first layer, you clearly state that you process personal data and for which purposes you do so.

In the first layer, you clearly state that you process personal data and for which purposes you do so. The second layer provides further explanation about the personal data and purposes. Ensure that for each purpose, it is clear what (type of) personal data is used, so that the website visitor can make an informed choice per purpose. When you use different purposes, you must enable the website visitor to give or withhold consent for each purpose. Ensure that the website visitor already has a general understanding of what the cookies mean for their personal data before giving consent. Any second layer is only intended to provide more detailed information: about which personal data is processed, and for what purposes. Do you share data with third parties for a specific purpose? Then you must clearly state in the first layer that you share data with third parties and the number of third parties. This helps the website visitor immediately make an initial assessment of the impact of the processing activities. To fully inform website visitors, you must also provide additional information. Indicate: what data you share; for which processing purposes you share this data; for each processing purpose, with which third parties you share this data. Consent Management Platform (CMP) Many website owners do not develop their cookie banners themselves but use a so-called Consent Management Platform (CMP). CMPs often offer additional functionalities, such as standard texts for processing purposes, an automatic scan of used cookies or plugins, and blocking data collection before consent has been received. Even if you outsource the setup of your cookie banner, it remains your responsibility to comply with the GDPR. In practice, the default settings of a CMP for a cookie banner often do not comply with the GDPR. Through the CMP's portal, you can often adjust the settings and design of the cookie banner. Cannot you adjust the settings of your CMP? Or can you not adjust the cookie banner in such a way that it complies with the GDPR? Then engage in dialogue with the CMP to ensure they take appropriate measures so that you can comply with the GDPR. If the CMP does not cooperate, you must take action yourself. For example, by switching to another CMP.

AP Netherlands - Clear cookie banners

ogue with the CMP to ensure they take appropriate measures so that you can comply with the GDPR. If the CMP does not cooperate, you must take action yourself. For example, by switching to another CMP. The fact that the CMP does not have something in proper order does not relieve you of your own responsibility to comply with the GDPR. Should you consider using a different CMP, the AP advises you to investigate beforehand whether this CMP allows you to configure your cookie banner in accordance with the GDPR. On this page, you will find the guidelines for designing a clear cookie banner. If you follow these guidelines and implement them correctly, you will have a cookie banner that complies with the GDPR. Legal Bases Consent The processing of personal data via tracking cookies must be based on the legal basis of consent. In doing so, ensure that: You obtain consent before placing such cookies. It must be clear to website visitors that you are asking for their consent with the cookie banner. Your website visitors must be able to give consent in a free, specific, informed, and unambiguous manner. Unambiguous means that it is very clear that someone has given consent. It is therefore obvious that your website visitors have a neutral choice, because all choices are equally easy to make. And that one option does not receive more emphasis than another. For more information about consent as a legal basis, refer to the EDPB guidelines on consent.

use all choices are equally easy to make. And that one option does not receive more emphasis than another. For more information about consent as a legal basis, refer to the EDPB guidelines on consent. Consider cookies that are necessary for the security of your website, or to enable the website to remember which products have been placed in the shopping cart. For more intrusive cookies, such as tracking cookies, the legal basis of legitimate interest is therefore not possible. The user must give consent. Why is a clear cookie banner important? What people do on the internet is very personal. Tracking cookies enable organizations to monitor the internet behavior of their website visitors. This is only permitted if website visitors explicitly agree to it. They must also have the option to reject such cookies without adverse consequences. With clear information about the use of such cookies, your website visitor can make an informed choice whether to give consent or not. Therefore, ensure a clear cookie banner, with which you will immediately comply with legal requirements. This also includes avoiding misleading methods ('dark patterns' or 'deceptive patterns') to obtain consent for cookies. For example, by making certain buttons less visible. Your website visitor then cannot make a proper choice.

If an organization does not comply with the rules, the AP can intervene. This also applies if an organization processes personal data with cookies and does not request consent in the correct manner. For example, by misleading website visitors. Since 2024, the AP has been more strictly monitoring the use of cookies. We more frequently check whether websites correctly request consent for cookies and other tracking software. Read more: This is how the AP supervises cookies. The guidelines for cookie banners apply to cookies and all other techniques with which you store information on or gain access to the user's device (such as a mobile phone or computer). What information should be on the first layer of my cookie banner? Certain information must be immediately visible in your cookie banner.

This way, your website visitor knows what the consent is for. Other information may, if appropriate given its conciseness, be placed on a second layer. AP Netherlands - Legal basis: Consent

**Legal basis for consent** If you want to collect and use personal data, you need a legal basis from the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). One of the GDPR legal bases is that individuals have given consent to process their personal data. On this page, you can read, among other things, what valid consent must meet, how to request consent, and how to demonstrate that you have obtained consent. **On this page** Requirements for consent The GDPR sets out several requirements that consent as a legal basis must meet. If consent does not meet these requirements, then the consent is not valid. You may not process the personal data. Consent must meet these requirements: * freely given; * specific; * informed; * unambiguous. **Freely given** Individuals must have given consent 'freely' (in freedom). This means that you may not pressure someone into giving consent. For example, by disadvantaging someone if they do not give consent. Pay attention to power imbalances. Employees, for instance, may find it difficult to refuse a request from their employer. **Unambiguous** There must be a clear affirmative action to give consent. For example, a (digital) written statement or an oral statement. It must be very clear in any case that consent has been given. You may not assume that someone gives implicit consent. Therefore, the use of pre-ticked boxes is not permitted.

AP Netherlands - Legal basis: Consent

nt or an oral statement. It must be very clear in any case that consent has been given. You may not assume that someone gives implicit consent. Therefore, the use of pre-ticked boxes is not permitted. **Informed** You must inform individuals in advance about: * your identity as an organisation; * the purpose of each processing operation for which you request consent; * which personal data you collect and use; * the right individuals have to withdraw consent. You must provide the information for requesting consent in an accessible form. The information must also be understandable, so that someone can make an informed choice. This means you must use clear and plain language. **Specific** Consent must always relate to a specific processing operation and a specific purpose. Do you have multiple purposes for processing data? Then you must inform individuals about this and request consent separately for each purpose. The purpose may not change over time. **Requesting consent** The GDPR does not precisely prescribe the form in which you must request consent. So you are free to choose how you request consent. One way to request consent is to have someone complete and sign a written statement. In an online environment, you can ask individuals to give consent by, for example: * actively ticking a box; * clicking on a button or a link; * filling out an electronic form; * sending you an email; * providing an electronic signature; * uploading a scanned document with a signature.

AP Netherlands - Legal basis: Consent

ctively ticking a box; * clicking on a button or a link; * filling out an electronic form; * sending you an email; * providing an electronic signature; * uploading a scanned document with a signature. An oral statement can also be sufficient to obtain valid consent. However, with this, it may be difficult for you to prove that you have actually obtained consent. For example, you can obtain consent with a recorded phone conversation. You must provide clear information in this case. And ask for specific confirmation from the individual. For example, that someone presses a button or clearly says 'yes' or 'no'. **Demonstrating that you have consent** According to the GDPR, you have an accountability obligation. To demonstrate valid consent, you must not only record the consent itself. You must also be able to show what information the individual was provided with when giving consent. Are you requesting online consent from individuals for processing their personal data? Then you can record information about the website visit during which they gave consent. You can combine this information with: * documentation about how you receive and record consent; * a copy of the information individuals received before giving consent. Finally, you must ensure that you have sufficient data to demonstrate a link between the processing and an individual's consent. Note that you may not collect more data than is necessary for this purpose.

Note that you may not collect more data than is necessary for this purpose. **Withdrawing consent** Individuals have the right to withdraw their consent. This must be as easy as giving consent. Therefore, ensure that individuals can easily withdraw their consent. What is not permitted, for example: individuals can give consent online with 1 click or swipe, but have to call customer service or send a letter if they want to withdraw their consent. **Consent concerning children** Do you want to process personal data of children? And do you want to do so based on consent as a legal basis? Then you must pay attention to these points: **Provide additional protection** The GDPR provides additional protection for children under 16 years of age. This is because children cannot or can less accurately assess the risks of data processing. **Ensure valid consent** Children under 16 years of age cannot validly give consent themselves for the processing of their data. Consent is only valid if one of the child's parents or guardians gives consent. And if you also meet the regular requirements for consent. **Consent for online processing** Do you process children's data online? For example, via an app, online game, webshop, or social media? Then you may only do this for children under 16 years of age with the consent of one of the parents or guardians.

So if you want to use children's personal data for marketing purposes or to create personality or user profiles. And also if you want to collect personal data about children when using services provided directly to children. It can be inferred from the GDPR that it is intended that no parental or guardian consent is required for support and advisory services offered directly and free of charge to children. See: Recital 38 of the GDPR. **Consent for offline processing** Do you process children's data offline? For example, for an order in a physical store? This too is only permitted for children under 16 years of age if one of the parents or guardians has given consent for it. **Verify who gave consent** According to the GDPR, you are obliged to verify whether consent has been given by one of the child's parents or guardians. You must be able to demonstrate this when the Dutch Data Protection Authority asks for it. Note: Are you targeting children in another EU country? Note: Does the law already stipulate that you may process special categories of personal data? Then you do not also need explicit consent. Explicit consent is an enhanced form of consent. Thus, explicit consent (Article 9 GDPR) is different from the 'normal', unambiguous consent which is one of the 6 legal bases for processing data (Article 6 GDPR). More is required for explicit consent than for unambiguous consent. The term 'explicit' refers to the way in which individuals express their consent. It is obvious that you achieve this with a written statement from that person. To avoid any doubt, you can also have it signed by that individual. But this is not the only way to obtain explicit consent. In a digital or online context, an individual can provide the required statement by filling in an electronic form, sending an email, uploading a scanned document with a signature, or providing an electronic signature.

nline context, an individual can provide the required statement by filling in an electronic form, sending an email, uploading a scanned document with a signature, or providing an electronic signature. You can also offer website visitors a screen where they can give their explicit consent by clicking 'yes' or 'no'. Note: The accompanying text must clearly formulate the consent. For example: 'I hereby give consent for the processing of [insert here which personal data are concerned].' You must also provide sufficient information to your visitors about what you do with their data if they give consent. In theory, an oral statement can also be sufficient, but it may be difficult for you to prove that you have met all conditions for valid explicit consent. For more information, consult the EDPB guidelines on consent, Chapter 4. **Consent concerning public authorities** Do you want to know if you, as a public authority, can use consent as a legal basis? This is usually not possible. Nevertheless, as a public authority, you may find yourself in a situation where requesting consent is desirable: you want to ensure that people in a vulnerable position receive help from other organisations. Below, you will read when valid consent may still be possible in such a situation. **Freely given** One of the requirements for consent is that it is freely given. Therefore, consent as a legal basis for public authorities is usually not possible. Citizens are usually dependent on public authorities.

AP Netherlands - Legal basis: Consent

ne of the requirements for consent is that it is freely given. Therefore, consent as a legal basis for public authorities is usually not possible. Citizens are usually dependent on public authorities. For example, when they apply for a facility from the municipality (see Recital 43 of the GDPR). **Legal basis for public authorities** Public authorities can therefore usually base the processing of personal data, when performing public tasks, on a legal basis specifically applicable to public authorities. That legal basis then follows from legislation. In such cases, the legislator must also ensure that the data is well protected: by carefully weighing what is necessary and also clearly determining what is and is not permitted (see Article 6, paragraph 1, point (e), and paragraph 3, of the GDPR). Requesting consent is therefore generally not necessary for a public authority and usually does not fit well into the relationship between citizen and government. Public authorities are therefore - rightly - reluctant in practice to request consent. **When consent is desirable** Nevertheless, as a public authority, you may find yourself in a situation where requesting consent is desirable. This concerns a situation where you want to provide personal data of people in a vulnerable position to other organisations, with whom these people are (probably) not yet familiar. So that these people can receive help from those organisations.

AP Netherlands - Legal basis: Consent

provide personal data of people in a vulnerable position to other organisations, with whom these people are (probably) not yet familiar. So that these people can receive help from those organisations. But where this provision is not necessary for the performance of your own legal task. The purpose of the GDPR is not to deprive free citizens of the opportunity to give consent for processing that is evidently - also according to the citizen themselves - in their own interest. On the other hand, legislation offers citizens protection. And it is not the intention that public authorities, outside these safeguards, under the guise of 'consent', are given the opportunity to impose unwanted processing on free citizens. Not even if it is clear that the intended help, according to the government or objectively, is in their interest. When, as a public authority, are you actually allowed to request consent in a situation where it is desirable? It is not the case that giving free consent to public authorities is, by definition, never possible. In certain situations, it is conceivable that genuinely free consent exists. You can then still provide the data based on consent. If someone gives you explicit consent, then you may also provide special categories of personal data. But when does such a situation occur? The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has created an overview of indications that a situation exists in which giving free consent to a public authority is possible.

AP Netherlands - Legal basis: Consent

hen does such a situation occur? The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has created an overview of indications that a situation exists in which giving free consent to a public authority is possible. **Indications for free consent for public authorities** The AP sees these indications for free consent given to a public authority: * The processing for which you request consent is in the interest of the data subject. * The processing is not (also) in your interest. * The safeguarding of that interest is not mandated to you. * You request consent in response to a concretely manifested request for help in an individual case. Privacy Risks and Protecting Your Privacy with Cookies Cookies can harm your privacy. Therefore, make a conscious choice when a website or app asks you to accept cookies. There are several ways to better protect your privacy from cookies. Below we explain what you can do yourself. On this page How cookies can harm your privacy Cookies collect information about your interests, behavior, and preferences. With this information, advertising companies can create a profile of you. Advertisers use people's profiles to display targeted advertisements on websites and apps. Advertisers can sell or share these profiles with other organizations. The more data companies have about you, the better they can estimate what you want to buy. Advertising companies can also influence you with this information. Thus, the (unconscious) acceptance of cookies ultimately leads to you seeing personalized ads. For example, companies can show you an offer exactly at the right moment that you are likely to find very attractive. Ads can persuade you to do certain things or buy products, even if you might not have intended to. Advertisers can therefore influence which products or services you buy. Examples of privacy risks from cookies. Cookies can collect information about relatively harmless topics. For example, do you frequently view sports articles on apps and websites? Then companies will categorize you as a 'sports enthusiast'.

GDPR general The most important law regarding the protection of personal data is the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This European law applies throughout the entire European Union (EU). Under this topic, you will find general information about the GDPR: how is the GDPR structured and what are its basic principles? On this page General information Legal text GDPR The consolidated legal text of the GDPR is the most convenient to use, as it incorporates subsequent changes (rectifications) to the original legal text. This version is a good representation of the current, amended text of the GDPR. The official legal text of the GDPR is the text as published in the Official Journal of the EU on 4 May 2016. This makes it the legally binding version of the GDPR. Two rectifications were subsequently published for this legal text: GDPR rectification of 23 May 2018, GDPR rectification of 4 March 2021. Further reading Quick answers Does the GDPR apply to pilots, tests, and trial projects? Yes. If you process personal data during a pilot, test, or trial project, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies. This is also true if the final product has not yet been delivered. This means, among other things, that you must determine whether you are permitted to process personal data. If so, you must demonstrate compliance with the GDPR. For example, you must assess whether you need to conduct a DPIA prior to a pilot, test, or trial project.

A pilot, test, or trial project can also be very useful for testing privacy by design. Does the GDPR apply to business cards I receive? If you systematically store business cards you receive (e.g., by saving them alphabetically) for professional use, then the GDPR applies. In such cases, you are strictly speaking the controller. This means you must base the processing of personal data on business cards on a legal basis. Consent In this case, you can base the processing on the legal basis of consent. You may assume that the person who gives you the business card also gives you consent to use the card for its intended purpose (storing and using contact details). You can easily demonstrate that you have received consent because you possess the card. AP Netherlands - Fine of 600,000 euros for tracking cookies on Kruidvat.nl

Fine of 600,000 euros for tracking cookies on Kruidvat.nl 16 July 2024 Themes: Cookies Big data and profiling The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has imposed a fine of 600,000 euros on the company behind drugstore Kruidvat. The reason for the fine is that the company tracked visitors to Kruidvat.nl using tracking cookies, without their knowledge or consent. In doing so, the company collected and used sensitive personal data of millions of website visitors in violation of the rules. The company behind Kruidvat, AS Watson (Health & Beauty Continental Europe) B.V., collected data from website visitors and could thereby create personal profiles of these individuals. In addition to visitors' location data, this included which pages they visited, which products they added to their shopping cart and purchased, and which recommendations they clicked on. This is very sensitive information due to the specific nature of drugstore products, such as pregnancy tests, contraceptives, or medication for various ailments. This sensitive information, linked to the location (which can potentially be traced via the IP address) of the unique visitor, can paint a very specific and invasive profile of the people visiting Kruidvat.nl. Aleid Wolfsen, chairman of the AP: 'With tracking cookies or tracking software, organisations can monitor your internet behaviour. This is not permitted without consent and without informing your customers. Because what you do online is very personal.

Tracking cookies without consent Kruidvat.nl should have requested consent from visitors before placing tracking cookies on their computers. The GDPR privacy law sets several requirements for valid consent. These requirements are that consent must be given freely, for a specific processing of personal data, based on sufficient information, and there must be no doubt that consent has been given. In the cookie banner on Kruidvat.nl, the boxes to agree to the placement of tracking software were pre-ticked by default. This is not allowed. Visitors who still wished to refuse the cookies had to go through many steps to achieve this. The AP has determined that personal data of Kruidvat.nl website visitors were unlawfully processed. Opportunity to rectify the situation At the end of 2019, the AP initiated an investigation into various websites, including Kruidvat.nl. The AP assessed whether these websites complied with the requirements for placing (tracking) cookies. The AP investigated whether consent for tracking cookies was requested from website visitors and, if so, how exactly this occurred.
